cards.front: Compute the CVA Problemfall scalar from standard-normal quantiles: \( \Phi^{-1}(0{,}95)/\Phi^{-1}(0{,}99) = 1{,}6449/2{,}3263 = \;?\)
A COREP CVA risk-exposure amount (PosNr 7516000) is €50.000.000. Apply the regulatory own-funds weight to get the CVA-Eigenmittelerfordernis (in EUR).
CVA-EM-Erfordernis = €4.000.000. Compute the CVA Problemfall figure (×0,71), in EUR.
CVA-EM-Erfordernis = €4.000.000. Compute the CVA Extremfall figure (×1,33), in EUR.

By the FIXED quantile ratio (NOT the Beteiligungsrisiko '3× rule'), by how much does the CVA Extremfall exceed the Problemfall? \( 1{,}33/0{,}71 = \Phi^{-1}(0{,}999)/\Phi^{-1}(0{,}95) = 3{,}0902/1{,}6449 = \;?\)
CVA risk = potential mark-to-market loss on derivative receivables caused by a {{c1}} of the counterparty's credit spread, the position {{c2}}.

Both CVA scalars are pure quantile ratios off the 99% base: \(0{,}71=\Phi^{-1}(0{,}95)/\Phi^{-1}(0{,}99)\) and \(1{,}33=\Phi^{-1}({{c1}})/\Phi^{-1}(0{,}99)\). The identical pair also rescales the trading-book {{c2}} (M6).
Derive the CVA Problemfall and Extremfall scalars from the regulatory base confidence.

steps.prompt: At what confidence is the standardised regulatory CVA charge calibrated?
steps.explain: The CRR Title VI standardised CVA charge is a 99% number — the fixed regulatory base.

steps.prompt: Under normality VaR_q = Φ⁻¹(q)·σ. Taking the ratio VaR_q2/VaR_q1, what happens to σ?
steps.explain: σ is confidence-independent, so re-scaling confidence is a pure ratio of standard-normal quantiles.

cards.front: In the CVA chain '8% × PosNr 7516000, then ×0,71 / ×1,33', classify each element as regulatory or ÖRS choice, and state the tradeoff the ÖRS part buys.
rubric: Names the regulatory-fixed elements: the CVA risk-exposure amount (PosNr 7516000), the 8% own-funds weight, and the 99% calibration confidence (all CRR Title VI).
Names the ÖRS choices: (1) importing the regulatory charge instead of modelling CVA, and (2) rescaling confidence by normal-quantile ratios (0,71 / 1,33).
Produces the tradeoff: the ÖRS scaling buys a one-multiplication, fully auditable, sector-standardisable figure at the cost of normal-tail accuracy.

cards.front: The Leitfaden imports the regulatory CVA charge rather than building its own CVA model. Reg-forced or ÖRS choice — and what is the tradeoff?
rubric: Identifies this as an ÖRS proportionality choice — the CRR does not force the bank to reuse the COREP charge inside the RTFA.

Produces the tradeoff: full CVA modelling needs per-netting-set expected-exposure profiles, counterparty CDS/proxy spreads and a sensitivity/simulation engine — data-hungry and impossible to standardise across ~400 Raiffeisenbanken.
Notes the justification: CVA is rarely the binding risk for a Raiffeisenbank, so the precision sacrificed is immaterial.

cards.front: A junior nets a DVA paper gain into the CVA figure and also books the counterparty's jump-to-default here. Which treatments are correct under the regulatory scope, and where does each risk belong?
rubric: CVA risk = spread-driven MTM loss with no default — that, and only that, belongs in this §5.2 charge.
Counterparty default (jump-to-default of the receivable) belongs in credit risk (M5) via the derivative's EAD/exposure; booking it here double-counts.
DVA (own-spread paper gain) is excluded from the regulatory CVA charge entirely — you may not net a 'gain' from your own deterioration into the figure.

cards.front: Defend, then critique, the normal-distribution assumption behind the 0,71 / 1,33 CVA scalars. Does 1,33 over- or under-state the extreme tail, and why is the simplification nonetheless defensible?

rubric.text: States the assumption: VaR = Φ⁻¹(q)·σ holds only under a normal/parametric distribution — that is exactly what lets σ cancel and makes the scaling a pure quantile ratio.
Direction of the error: real credit spreads are fat-tailed (they gap/jump in stress), so the true 99,9%/99% quantile ratio EXCEEDS 1,33 — therefore 1,33 may UNDERSTATE the genuine extreme tail.
Defends the tradeoff: a one-multiplication, fully auditable, proportional scaling, justified because CVA is rarely the binding risk for a Raiffeisenbank.
Contrasts op-risk (M8), which deliberately blends a lognormal precisely to respect tails, showing the normal shortcut here was a conscious choice.

antiPoints: Claiming the assumption is lognormal, or that 1,33 OVERstates the tail.
cards.modelAnswer: The scalars rest on VaR = Φ⁻¹(q)·σ, valid only under normality; that is exactly what lets σ cancel so re-scaling confidence becomes the pure quantile ratio Φ⁻¹(0,999)/Φ⁻¹(0,99) = 1,33. But credit spreads are fat-tailed — they gap and jump in stress — so the true 99,9%/99% ratio is larger than 1,33, meaning 1,33 may understate the genuine extreme tail of CVA risk. The simplification is nonetheless defensible: it delivers a single, fully auditable multiplication that is standardisable across the sector, and CVA is rarely the binding risk for a Raiffeisenbank. That the Leitfaden blends a lognormal for op-risk (M8) shows the normal shortcut here was a conscious proportionality call, not an oversight.

cards.front: Explain why 0,71 and 1,33 have 'nothing intrinsically to do with CVA', where else the identical machinery appears, and what the CRR III flag changes.
cards.sourceNote: The CRR III BA-CVA/SA-CVA recalibration post-dates the Leitfaden 09/2024 (EU application 1 Jan 2025); verify against current EUR-Lex / EBA. The 0,71/1,33 scaling step itself is unaffected.

rubric.text: States they are general vertical-consistency scalars — Φ⁻¹(0,95)/Φ⁻¹(0,99) and Φ⁻¹(0,999)/Φ⁻¹(0,99) — pure confidence-rescaling off a 99% base, with nothing CVA-specific.
Gives the reuse: the trading-book Preisrisiko (M6) uses the IDENTICAL 0,71 / 1,33; op-risk (M8) the same idea on a 99,9% anchor, but with a mixed normal/lognormal (giving 5,0%).

CRR III flag: the standardised CVA method is replaced by BA-CVA / SA-CVA (EU application 1 Jan 2025), so the risk-exposure amount behind PosNr 7516000 is recalibrated — but the 0,71/1,33 scaling is unaffected because it is pure quantile arithmetic.

antiPoints: Treating 0,71 as a CVA-specific haircut set by CRR Title VI.
Claiming CRR III changes the 0,71 / 1,33 scalars themselves.
cards.modelAnswer: 0,71 and 1,33 are not CVA constants — they are general vertical-consistency factors, Φ⁻¹(0,95)/Φ⁻¹(0,99) and Φ⁻¹(0,999)/Φ⁻¹(0,99), that rescale any VaR off a 99% base under normality. The same machinery drives the trading-book Preisrisiko in M6 (the identical 0,71 / 1,33) and, conceptually, op-risk in M8 — though op-risk anchors at 99,9% and blends a lognormal, giving its 5,0% factor instead. Under CRR III the standardised CVA framework is replaced by BA-CVA / SA-CVA from 1 Jan 2025, recalibrating the risk-exposure amount behind PosNr 7516000; the scaling step is unaffected because it is pure quantile arithmetic. So memorise the formula, not the numbers.
